correctness.rationale: Five-variable affine-determinant expansion forces every positive support product to a same-oriented extremal original quintuple; their strict 2-square/3-pentagon pattern excludes mixed supports. Euclidean strict convexity fixes each square point to an adjacent original square vertex. Maximal pentagon vertex triangles are five cyclic gap (1,2,2) triples; a vertex lies in exactly three, so two independently variable supports would force four maximal triples through a fixed vertex and are impossible. Exactly five allowable edge motions form C5 for each of the four square choices. All 126 vertex quintuples and all 31^3 pentagon support systems were checked by the included exact Q(sqrt(5)) checker; unlimited-point equality follows analytically, not from enumeration.

originality.rationale: Compared equivalent objects, stricter or broader settings and the exact published nine-vertex simplex spectrum. That record explicitly disclaims the nonvertex equality classification; Medgyes proves only the containing polytope. The known 2017 regular-pentagon sliding triangle construction supplies planar precursor, but not the four-dimensional all-points rigidity, simultaneous-motion exclusion and four-component optimizer topology. A distinct ten-vertex equal-regular-pentagon free sum has a connected equality graph, not this result. No directly covering theorem was identified; priority remains provisional.
residual_risks: An unindexed general theorem about equality loci of maximal simplices in orthogonal polygon sums might subsume the result.
The planar triangle sliding construction is an old fact; the four-dimensional topology is new only insofar as exhaustive mixed-support and multi-motion exclusions were not already published.
Historical priority is provisional without independent expert literature review.

value.rationale: Natural complete equality-case classification for the uniquely volume-optimal nine-vertex four-polytope. The preexisting discrete twenty-maximizer table conceals twenty continuous slide families arranged as FOUR disconnected circles, unlike the connected ten-vertex case. The signed-support structural lemma rules out all other arbitrary-point optimizers and explains the full global topology; this is more than an extra numerical invariant or routine vertex census. Its narrow scope and reliance on known planar triangle movement are explicit.
